Guides

Cooking and seasoning

Herbs, a mild spice, and a spoonful of oil do more for a baby’s food than salt or sugar ever will.

Findings

No added salt before one year. That includes the cooking water, the stock, and the ‘pinch’ in a pasta sauce.
Sweetness can come from fruit. Added sugar is unnecessary before two years, and honey is unsafe before one.
Cook for the family, then season the grown-ups’ plates. Take out your baby’s portion before salt, chilli, or a salty sauce goes in.

Salt

A baby’s kidneys can’t handle much sodium, and salty food builds a taste for salt that’s hard to undo. The simple rule: no salt in cooking for a child under one. Cheese, bread, and tinned foods already contain some, so keep those to small amounts.

Stock cubes, gravy, ham, bacon, soy sauce, and most ‘baby seasonings’ that list salt are grown-up shortcuts. Your own unsalted stock, frozen in cubes, is a different thing entirely.

Sugar, honey, and spice

Added sugar pushes out iron-rich foods and feeds tooth decay as soon as teeth come through. Fruit, roasted pumpkin, and ripe banana are sweet enough for biscuits and porridge. Honey isn’t a more natural choice under one: botulism spores survive ordinary baking.

Sweet paprika, turmeric, cumin, oregano, basil, and a pinch of cinnamon are all fine. Hot chilli and lots of black pepper are not. Keep cinnamon to a pinch, not a spoonful: cassia cinnamon contains coumarin.

One pot for everyone

Stews, sauces, and roasts can feed the whole household if you lift out the baby’s share first. Mash theirs or cut it to a texture they can manage. Then salt yours.

Garlic and onion cooked into the dish are fine. Garlic or herbs kept in a jar of oil are not: that’s a known botulism risk. Add fresh herbs and oil at the end of cooking.
